Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: In the United States, is it wrong to address a full professor as "doctor"?
Answer: At some institutions, people are flattered if you call them something other than “hey, you!” At least in my lab, we were on a first-name basis with the boss, though it took me a really long time to get comfortable with that. Might be a California/Caltech thing, where *maybe* you address a Nobel Laureate as “Professor”, but sometimes not. In general, I don’t know too many people who would get insulted if you called them “doctor” rather than “professor”, and frankly, if they did get offended, they need to get over themselves. The only time I see “Dr. Kozlowski” is on a formal performance review, or formal correspondence from people I don’t know.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why is it that majority of PhD holders are giving scary testimonies about their experience, so making prospective PhD students even more scared about going for PhD? What exactly is the most scary part of PhD?
Answer: The scariest part of your PhD is the sense that your entire career path and fate rests on the whims of a small group of people (your boss most of all, and your thesis committee to a certain extent). If your boss tells you to go jump in a lake, the expectation is that you will do it. You can come up with an elegant Grand Unified Theory of Everything which turns out to be right, and if your thesis committee gets a bee in its bonnet, it can prevent you from graduating. (Dan Shechtman proposed the idea of a quasi-crystal, and was asked to leave his research group for coming up with a concept that was considered so incredibly idiotic, it was an embarrassment to have him in the group. Shechtman got the last laugh, though, winning the Nobel Prize in 2011. Had he had this idea as a graduate student, he would never have been able to publish it). Emotional abuse by advisers towards their students is so commonplace, it’s considered part of the experience. In our institution, there was a case of a professor sexually harassing one of his students, and behaving in an unprofessional manner with another one of them. Both of those students did end up getting a settlement, I think, but their careers were ruined, and they had to finish their PhDs at another institution. Now, you can get lucky and have a boss who is compassionate, patient, and wise (I was lucky in this way), but if you’re working for a jerk, your choices are to either tough it out, transfer, or drop out. The other thing that’s scary about a PhD is that there is no definite end date, and no really good way of measuring your progress. If you are in high school or college, you know you have to pass X classes in order to graduate. Not so with graduate school, and your boss is very much setting the standard for what it takes to graduate. That standard is opaque, and can shift. Worse, there is nothing that says you can’t be in a program for 3 years, start making some decent progress…..and then your adviser pulls the plug, and you have to hope that somebody else will hire/mentor you. There’s this constant nagging sense of “am I really good enough?”, which a sociopathic mentor will exploit. As to the other part of the question, why do people give scary testimonies: in large part, because they are true. There are people who have had good experiences working towards a PhD (I’m one of them, even though I had some rough patches). But also a lot of bad stories out there. One thing a PhD *should* instill is a sense of rigor and intellectual honesty. If I’m being rigorous and intellectually honest, I shouldn’t sugar-coat things.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: My essay got 1% similarity in Turnitin, but my professor still says it’s plagiarism. What should I do?
Answer: I would say, “OK, point to the exact passage that Turnitin says was copied.” A lot of these plagiarism detectors will flag specific instances of suspected plagiarism. If you lifted a sentence or two verbatim from another source, you might be in trouble, because lifting even a sentence or two is technically plagiarism. (Also depends how long this assignment is: is it a master’s thesis, or an essay? Also depends on what the sentence says. If it’s something like “Grass is green”, there really aren’t any ways to paraphrase that). I would go to the dean or the chair of your department, and insist on a formal hearing. You probably have a right to such a thing. The community college where I worked had a very elaborate system for dealing with allegations of cheating or other academic misconduct. I got to learn all about it, unfortunately, because I busted some of my students for copying off of each other in the early days of COVID where I was relying on the honor system. When I leveled the accusation, I had specific, compelling evidence (I lined up *several* suspect answers *across multiple tests*, and in several cases they were practically photocopies of each other). The students had the right to 1) know the specific accusation being made against them, 2) see the evidence being presented in support of that accusation, 3) retain legal counsel if they so desired and 4) to convene a formal hearing to determine whether or not sanctions should be imposed. I don’t remember whether the evidential standard was “preponderance of evidence” or “clear and compelling evidence”, because the students basically took a plea deal when they saw the evidence I had, but there was an evidential standard. I was very impressed that the college did this. If I were sitting on the board or tribunal that was deciding such a case, there would be four things I would want to know. 1) What is the *specific* passage in question? I’m not convinced by a 1% similarity: what *exactly* was copied? 2) What is the *length* of the passage in question? A sentence fragment? A sentence? A whole paragraph? 3) Is the passage cited? I would look much more sympathetically on a case where the passage was perhaps missing quotation marks, but the credit was clearly given. 4) How easily could the passage in question be paraphrased?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the benefits of completing a Ph.D.?
Answer: The PhD is not a degree that displays your brilliance, or even a reasonable intelligence: the PhD is a stubbornness degree. I don’t think I’m especially bright, but I ground it out for 6 years. The biggest benefit is knowing that I can buckle down and deal with years of discouraging results if I have to. Completing a PhD also makes you a little more modest. I got roughed up by my thesis committee during candidacy. When I finished my thesis, I thought, “wow, I thought this was going to be longer/more important/cooler.” I definitely saw other people in my program produce better work. So, the process got me off my high horse. When you’re working at the leading edge, you get to see new discoveries every day by following the literature. And the requirement for getting a PhD is that you discovered something new. There’s a very real satisfaction in being able to say “I’m the first person ever to do X.” That’s really cool. The training provided by a PhD is, or should be, an antidote to the types of non-thinking that are common in our age of misinformation, bluster, and overall baloney. During a PhD you have to ask yourself, what do we know, and how do we know it? What is the mechanism for something to be working in a particular way? And, do I have enough information and evidence to conclude what I’m about to conclude? This runs contrary to the trends of today, where people frequently say, “I know X to be true because my favorite politician/pundit/random guy on Facebook said it. I’m not going to worry about how X could possibly be true, or look for evidence running in the other direction.” This sort of trained skepticism is especially important during COVID, when a lot of discussion is on scientific topics. At least in chemistry, your career is limited if you have just a BS. To get a position with more responsibility and better pay, you kind of need an MS or a PhD.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How can you determine if a professor has written a PhD thesis on a specific topic before beginning your own research?
Answer: You really shouldn’t be looking through other PhD theses in order to determine if your idea is novel….the thesis itself is kind of a formality. What you *should* be doing is looking through a huge stack of journal articles, and seeing if anyone has done your idea first. If you find something that looks a lot like your thesis idea in another article, ask yourself, “did they capture the whole story? Is there some follow-on work that needs to be done? Is this even a good paper?” Basically, Google Scholar and Web of Science (or another search engine) are your friends. Do a thorough literature search before you start your project!
